messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Mariana was twenty-three when she walked into the dimly lit chemical storage room in the basement of her university’s science building. It was late, just before closing time, and she needed to restock a few reagents for the organic chemistry lab she taught as a graduate assistant. The overhead fluorescent flickered and then went out, leaving only the faint glow from the hallway. She reached for the wall switch, but her hand brushed against a metal drum that had been left precariously near the edge of a shelf. It tipped. The cap wasn’t sealed. A colorless, acrid liquid splashed across her arms and chest, and the fumes hit her throat like a wall of fire. She gasped, stumbled backward, and her vision blurred. The next thing she knew, she was on the concrete floor, her lungs seizing, her skin burning. A janitor found her minutes later, but those minutes felt like hours of suffocation.

The paramedics arrived, and she remembers the bright lights of the ambulance, then the antiseptic smell of the emergency room, the sting of oxygen masks, the cold of a hospital bed. Her arms were treated for chemical burns, and she spent two days in observation for inhalation injuries. Medically, she recovered. But the sense of her body as something that had turned on her, that had nearly killed her, never left.

In the months afterward, Mariana found herself unable to explain what had happened. When friends asked, she could picture the moment: the drum, the darkness, the burn. But words stuck in her throat. She knew the story but could not arrange it in order—was the smell first or the pain? Did she scream? The sequence refused to line up, and when she tried to force it, a raw, burning sensation pulsed in her chest and along her forearms, as if the chemical were still eating into her skin. She stopped trying to talk about it. Instead, she tried to erase it entirely, pushing the images away so hard that she felt exhausted by the effort. She stopped going near the science building, found a longer route to her apartment that avoided that part of campus entirely.

But the world kept reminding her. At night, she would wake in complete darkness, her heart slamming, certain the air was turning toxic. She began sleeping with a lamp on, but even then, the moment she opened her eyes in the small hours, the panic was already there. During the day, she found herself scanning every room she entered—her classroom, the library, the grocery store—looking for spills, leaks, anything out of place. If a classmate touched her shoulder unexpectedly, she jerked away with a sharp gasp, which embarrassed her and made people think she was on edge. Her body stayed coiled, her shoulders hunched, her jaw tight, as if waiting for the next chemical attack. She told herself she was overreacting, but the physical reactions happened anyway: her hands would tremble, her breath would shorten, whenever she caught a whiff of hand sanitizer or passed a hospital.

Mariana had always thought of herself as capable and independent. Now she felt fundamentally broken. She had come to believe there was something wrong with her as a person—not just that she’d been in an accident, but that her own body had betrayed her. It kept reacting as if she were still in that storage room, as if the danger were still there, even when she knew rationally that she was safe. She no longer trusted her own lungs, her own skin. Every twinge or ache felt like the start of another poisoning.

The consequences crept into her daily life. She had taken a leave of absence from her graduate program because she could not enter the science building, and her supervisor did not understand why she would not switch to a different lab on another floor. Her social circle shrank; she declined invitations to movie nights because the dark theater would trigger her, and she avoided restaurants with strong cleaning smells. She felt isolated, ashamed, and convinced that she was failing at being a normal twenty-six-year-old.

What finally brought Mariana to the clinic was a panic attack during a routine doctor’s appointment. The antiseptic odor hit her the moment she walked in, and within seconds she was shaking, unable to speak, her memory dissolving into fragments of that Friday night. The physician referred her for psychological help. Mariana is terrified that nothing will make the body memories stop. But she is also, somewhere beneath the fear, hoping that maybe she can learn to sleep with the lights off again—and to trust that her own body is not her enemy.
